title: Countable nouns with a/an and some
subtitle: a dog / some dogs
summary: Use a/an with singular countable nouns and some with plural ones - and know when the plural noun is better used alone.

lesson.heading: Singular and plural
lesson.text: Countable nouns can be singular or plural. Before a singular countable noun you can use **a/an**. You cannot use a singular countable noun alone, without a/the/my etc.

lesson.heading: Saying what kind of thing or person
lesson.text: We use **a/an ...** to say what kind of thing something is, or what kind of person somebody is. In the plural we use the noun alone, without some.

lesson.heading: Compare singular and plural
rows: Jane and Ben are **really nice people**.

lesson.heading: Describing people and jobs
lesson.text: We say that somebody **has a long nose / a nice face / blue eyes / long fingers**. We also use **a/an** when we say what somebody's job is.

examples.text: Would you like to be **an English teacher**?

lesson.heading: some = a number of / a few of
lesson.text: You can use **some** with plural countable nouns to mean *a number of, a few of, a pair of*. Often you can say the same thing with or without some.

examples.text: **Some friends** of mine are coming to stay at the weekend.
The room was empty apart from a table and **(some) chairs**.

lesson.note: Do not use some when you are talking about things in general: I love **bananas** (not some bananas). My aunt is a writer. She writes **books** (not some books).

lesson.heading: some = some but not all
lesson.text: **Some** can also mean *some but not all*.

examples.text: Tomorrow there will be rain in **some places**, but most of the country will be dry.

lesson.text: Before you write *some*, ask: do I mean *a number of these* or *these in general*? Only the first one takes some.

exercises.explanation: A singular countable noun that says what kind of thing something is takes a/an.

exercises.prompt: The Nile, the Rhine and the Mekong are ___.
exercises.explanation: In the plural we use the noun alone, not some rivers.
Insect begins with a vowel sound, so we use an.

exercises.prompt: Read what these people do and match each one with their job.

pairs.left: Gary works in a restaurant. He brings the food to the tables.
Jane writes articles for a newspaper.
Kevin works in a hospital. He operates on people.
Dave installs and repairs water pipes.
Anna shows visitors round her city and tells them about it.
Lisa translates what people say from one language into another.

exercises.explanation: A singular countable noun cannot stand alone: a careful driver.

exercises.prompt: Mark works in a bookshop. He sells ___.
exercises.explanation: This is books in general, so no some.

exercises.statement: I've been walking for hours. I've got some sore feet.
exercises.explanation: I've got sore feet. Here we are simply saying what kind of feet they are, so we use the plural noun alone.

exercises.prompt: I don't feel very well. I've got ___.
exercises.explanation: Throat is a singular countable noun, so it needs a.

exercises.prompt: It might rain. Don't go out without ___.
exercises.explanation: Umbrella begins with a vowel sound: an umbrella.

exercises.prompt: ___ people learn languages more easily than others.
exercises.explanation: Some people = some but not all people.

exercises.prompt: Those are ___ shoes. Where did you get them?
exercises.explanation: We are saying what kind of shoes they are, so the plural noun is used alone.

exercises.prompt: What is missing in each sentence: a/an, some, or nothing at all?

items.text: When I was ___ child, I used to be very shy.
Would you like to be ___ actor?
I didn't expect to see you. What ___ surprise!
___ birds, for example the penguin, cannot fly.
You need a visa to visit ___ countries, but not all of them.
Questions, questions! You're always asking ___ questions!
Do you like staying in ___ hotels?
